excerpt: Clara's carefully picked happy graduation vapor banners hang too low from the adobe doors.
74th and Columbus, apartment 9D. Stephen Perdue watches his wife get ready for her violin lesson.
Oh man, did I blow the surprise?
He turns on CNN.
She takes out more bottles of wine from the cupboard.
Inside the cab, Margaret holds on to her violin case.
The congratulations sign still hits him on the back.
How could you do this to me?
Alexander and Margaret walk down Broadway.
Crusted chili, soap, bubbles, scrub.
Alexander pays for their hot dogs with crumpled up dollar bills he pulls out of his pocket.
Her eyes find his wallet right by the couch.
Across town, Gary sits at his art studio, drawing photo prints, moldy coffee cups.
Margaret walks away from this mess and into the living room, pours herself a large glass of red wine.
When the phone rings, Clara's throwing up.
He stands in his pajamas by the light of the open fridge.
Next time you blink, Clara, you'll be throwing away the last 20 and then 25 years of your life.
In Clara's closet, there's a huge stack of Gary's greeting cards, meticulously drawn.
She opens the pullout couch, uses 800 thread sheets to make it feel nice.
Gary is on the attack and she hates him.
They're making Sasha's bed on the pullout couch, new sheets, a festive Indian bedspread.
Clara puts the birthday card in an envelope and walks out into the night.
A leftover piece of blue crepe paper dangles from the Adobe kitchen frame.
In Alexander's apartment, the bathroom door is all glass, frosted glass.
Gary chooses a gorgeous funeral wreath, all orchids, all elegance.
The bar is half dark, stinks of grief, sweat, and wine.
The bathroom is full of wet steam.
For a moment, on 74th and Columbus, apartment 9D, there's a mother and daughter.
Two months later, October 2001, New York City.
Gary's mom cuts a thick slice of coffee cake.
Clara walks the empty Walmart aisles.
Stephen opens the door of his office to lead out a patient, and Clara's right there, waiting on the soft maroon couch.
On the TV, the Middle East, India, wars, earthquakes, crashes.
She eats his homemade chili, always better than hers, always soothing. Served in rustic pottery, not plastic.
Bach's second violin concerto fills the apartment as if Margaret's playing.
Sasha walks into Alexander's offices.
Clara takes an electric candle out of a Halloween lantern.
On 30th Street and First Avenue, the rain beats fast against the chalk white canvas.
When Clara heads to the airport, it is not yet dawn.
